title: Sources and uses: the budget is a promise
summary: A development budget has two sides that must balance: where the money comes from and where it goes. This lesson teaches the four cost buckets of a pro forma, how contingency works, and why every estimate must carry its class.
body:
A development budget is not a guess about cost. It is a promise that every dollar the project will spend has a named source, and that the two columns, sources and uses, add to the same number.

Recall

Q. In owner accounting, why do you track costs as you incur them rather than only when you pay the invoice?

A. Because accrual accounting records the obligation when it arises. A contractor's completed work is a cost the project owes even if the cheque has not gone out, and a budget that only counts payments will always look healthier than it is.

Q. What is the difference between cash and profit?

A. Profit is an accounting result over a period. Cash is what is actually in the bank. A project can show a paper profit and still run out of cash, which is why developers watch both.

Q. What does "bottom line first" mean in communication?

A. Lead with the conclusion, then give the reasons. A lender who hears the answer in the first sentence listens to the rest with less suspicion.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every financing conversation you will ever have starts with one page: the sources and uses. The lender reads it to decide how much to lend. The investor reads it to decide how much equity is at risk. The contractor reads it, if you let them, to judge whether you can pay. If that page is wrong, every decision built on it is wrong, and the error does not show itself until the money is half spent and the gap has nowhere to come from.

A pro forma is a projection of a project's costs, revenues and returns. This week covers the cost side. Next week covers revenue. The week after covers returns.

Uses: the four buckets

Uses is where the money goes. Professionals sort it into four buckets, and the discipline is to make sure every cost lands in exactly one of them.

  • Land. The purchase price plus the costs of acquiring it: legal fees, land transfer taxes where they apply, survey, title work.
  • Hard costs. Everything physically built: site work, foundations, structure, envelope, mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems, finishes. In short, what the general contractor and trades are paid for.
  • Soft costs. Everything needed to design, approve, sell and manage the building that is not bricks and mortar: architects, engineers, permits and development charges, insurance, legal, accounting, marketing, leasing commissions, and the developer's own fee.
  • Finance costs. The cost of borrowing during construction: lender fees, interest on the loan as it is drawn, and the reserve set aside to pay that interest before the building earns income.

The plain-English test for any line item is simple: if I removed this cost, would something physical be missing? If yes, it is hard. If no, it is soft, unless it is the price of money, in which case it is finance.

Sources: where the money comes from

Sources lists every dollar that will pay for those uses. In a simple project there are two: the construction loan and the owner's equity. Larger projects add mezzanine debt, government grants, pre-sale deposits that may be released to the project, or a joint-venture partner's equity. The professional rule is absolute: total sources must equal total uses, to the dollar. A sources and uses table that does not balance is not a draft. It is a funding gap with a page around it.

Here is a worked example. All numbers are hypothetical.

UsesAmount
Land, including acquisition costs3,000,000
Hard costs15,000,000
Hard cost contingency, 5 percent750,000
Soft costs3,000,000
Soft cost contingency, 5 percent150,000
Finance costs1,600,000
Total uses23,500,000
SourcesAmount
Construction loan, 65 percent of cost15,275,000
Owner's equity8,225,000
Total sources23,500,000

Read it aloud: twenty-three and a half million dollars of uses, funded by fifteen point two seven five million of debt and eight point two two five million of equity. The 65 percent figure is a loan-to-cost ratio. That ratio is commercial practice set by each lender, not a standard, and it varies with the market and the borrower.

Say that out loud now.

Contingency and estimate classes

Contingency is money in the budget for costs that will happen but cannot yet be named. It is not padding and it is not profit. A building always produces surprises: rock where the borehole showed clay, a supplier price rise, a coordination clash between the duct and the beam. Contingency is how the budget absorbs them without a crisis.

How much contingency you need depends on how much you know, and that is what an estimate class tells you. An estimate class is a label describing how mature the design and the information behind a cost estimate are. AACE International, a professional body for cost engineers, publishes a classification that runs from Class 5, a concept-stage figure built from a few comparable projects, to Class 1, an estimate built from a nearly complete design and real quotes. The published accuracy ranges for the earliest class are wide enough that the final cost could land well below the figure or roughly double it. Verify the current ranges against AACE's recommended practice before you rely on them.

Second worked example. Suppose an architect gives you a concept-stage figure of 15,000,000 for hard costs on a building that exists only as a massing model. If you put a 5 percent contingency on that number, you are pretending to Class 2 knowledge with Class 5 information. A sensible owner at that stage would carry a much larger design contingency, perhaps 15 to 20 percent of hard costs, as a hypothetical practice figure, and shrink it as drawings mature. At 15 percent, contingency becomes 2,250,000 instead of 750,000, and total uses rise by 1,500,000. That 1,500,000 is not waste. It is the honest price of not yet knowing.

The professional habit is to carry two contingencies and label them. Design contingency covers the design still growing. Construction contingency covers what goes wrong in the field after the contract is signed. Mixing them hides which risk you are actually carrying.

How the best do it

Turner Construction publishes a quarterly Building Cost Index tracking construction cost movement in the United States. The lesson for a small developer is not the index itself but the habit behind it: large builders keep their own historical cost data, per square metre and per trade, and test every new estimate against what similar buildings actually cost. You can copy that from your first project. At closeout, record the final cost by bucket, per square metre and per unit, with the date. After three projects you will own a reference set no consultant can sell you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a budget presented without its class. A Class 5 number travels from a sketch meeting into a lender's file and gets treated as a committed cost. The control is a header on every budget page stating the estimate class, the date, the drawing set it is based on, and the contingency carried. Professional sign-off required: a cost consultant or quantity surveyor should prepare or review any budget a lender will rely on.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets finance costs, or treats them as an afterthought. Interest during construction is real money, it rises with delay, and it is usually funded by the loan itself, which means it increases the loan. A budget that omits it does not balance once the first draw is made.

Callback

In Week 10 you learned that yield on cost is stabilised net operating income divided by total project cost. Every dollar you leave out of uses makes yield on cost look better than it is. A missing finance line of 1,600,000 on this project would flatter yield on cost by roughly seven percent of its value. The denominator is only honest if the sources and uses is.

Recap

Uses has four buckets: land, hard, soft and finance. Sources must equal uses to the dollar. Contingency is money for costs you cannot yet name, sized to the estimate class, which describes how much you actually know. Label every budget with its class and date.

Next: Ford takes you through a public building whose early figure was mistaken for a budget.
checklist: Total sources equal total uses to the dollar
Every cost sits in exactly one bucket: land, hard, soft or finance
Finance costs include fees, construction interest and the interest reserve
The budget page states its estimate class, date and drawing set
Design and construction contingency are carried and labelled separately
Contingency is sized to the estimate class, not to a habit
A cost consultant has reviewed any budget a lender will rely on
Closeout actuals are recorded per square metre and per unit for future projects
head: Field checklist
speak: The bottom line: a development budget is a promise that every dollar spent has a named source, and the two columns must balance to the dollar. Uses sorts into four buckets. Land is the site and the cost of buying it. Hard costs are everything physically built. Soft costs are design, approvals, insurance, legal, marketing and fees. Finance costs are lender fees and the interest paid while the building earns nothing. Sources is where the money comes from, usually a construction loan and owner's equity. Contingency is money for costs that will happen but cannot yet be named, and its size depends on the estimate class, which tells you how mature the design is. A concept-stage number needs a large contingency; a priced, nearly complete design needs less. So every budget I show carries its class, its date and its drawing set on the same page. That is how a lender knows how far to trust it.
terms: Sources and uses — a two-column table showing where every dollar of a project comes from and where it goes, with both columns adding to the same total.
Estimate class — a label describing how mature the design and information behind a cost estimate are, which sets how accurate it can be.
Contingency — money carried in the budget for costs that will happen but cannot yet be identified.

hostile.q: Your contingency is 5 percent of hard costs. Why should I believe that is enough?
hostile.a: Because it matches the stage we are at. The hard costs come from a priced estimate against a design that is substantially complete, prepared by an independent cost consultant whose report you have. Design contingency has been largely spent into the estimate; the 5 percent is construction contingency for field conditions. If you want a different number, I would rather discuss the specific risk you see, ground conditions or a trade price, than argue about the percentage.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman on finance
title: Holyrood: when an early figure became the budget
summary: The Scottish Parliament building at Holyrood was opened in 2004 at a cost roughly ten times the early figure first put to the public. This lesson takes the case through seven steps and draws one rule about how estimates must travel.
body:
The Scottish Parliament building did not overrun a budget so much as it never had one. An early range was published before a design existed, and every later number was measured against it.

Recall

Q. What does a schedule of values do in owner accounting?

A. It breaks the contract sum into line items so that progress and payment can be measured item by item, instead of as one lump that hides where the money is going.

Q. What is the time value of money?

A. The idea that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, because today's dollar can be invested or used. It is why delay costs money even when no invoice changes.

Q. What is the pyramid principle?

A. Put the main conclusion at the top, support it with a few grouped reasons, and put the detail underneath. The reader can stop at any level and still have the point.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the most dangerous number in development is the first one. It is usually produced fast, from a sketch, to answer the question "roughly what would it cost?" Then it is written down, repeated, and eventually treated as a commitment by people who never saw how thin it was. Holyrood is the clearest public example of that drift. The facts below are drawn from the public record, including the inquiry led by Lord Fraser of Carmyllie, whose report was published in 2004. Verify specific figures against that report before you cite them.

Step 1: Timeline

  • 1997: Scotland votes in a referendum for a devolved parliament. Early government documents put the cost of a new parliament building in a range from about ten to forty million pounds.
  • 1998: The Holyrood site is chosen and the architect Enric Miralles, working with a Scottish practice, wins the design competition.
  • Construction starts under a construction management arrangement while design is still developing.
  • 2000: Miralles dies in July. Donald Dewar, the First Minister who had championed the project, dies in October.
  • Costs are revised upward repeatedly over the following years.
  • 2004: The building opens. The final cost reported is around four hundred and fourteen million pounds. The Fraser inquiry reports in September.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions shaped the outcome. First, choosing a site and an architect before the brief, meaning the owner's written statement of what the building must contain and achieve, was settled. Second, choosing construction management, a delivery method in which the owner contracts directly with many trade packages and a manager coordinates them, which keeps cost risk with the owner. Third, starting construction while the design was still evolving, so packages were let against incomplete information.

Step 3: Assumptions

The central assumption was that the early figure described the building that would be built. It did not. It was a concept-stage number for a smaller, simpler building than the one eventually designed. In the language of Day 1, it was at best a Class 5 figure, and it was treated as if it were Class 2. The second assumption was that speed would save money. Starting early under construction management was meant to compress the programme. Instead it exposed the client to every design change as a priced change.

Step 4: Incentives

There was political pressure to deliver a landmark quickly for a new institution. Nobody in a public role wanted to be the person who announced a figure ten times larger at the start. The design ambition grew, the floor area grew, and each increase was defensible on its own. Under construction management, the people placing packages were not the people carrying the cost risk, so no party had a strong incentive to stop the drift.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The inquiry described cost information that did not reach decision-makers clearly, and repeated upward revisions treated as one-off events rather than a pattern. Each revision was a warning sign: if the number moves every quarter, the estimate class has not improved, whatever the drawings look like. A second sign was the growth in the building's size and complexity without a matching reset of the budget baseline.

Step 6: Point of no return

Once trade packages were let and construction was underway on a design still developing, the owner could no longer change the procurement route or the design without paying for the work already done and the delay caused. In a private project the equivalent moment is the first lender draw: from then on, every redesign is paid for twice.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was not the architect, the site or the deaths of the two men who championed it, though those made everything harder. The root cause was that an early figure was allowed to stand as a budget, with no stated class, no stated scope and no stated contingency, and the owner retained cost risk through the procurement route without the controls to manage it.

Translating it to a private project

Here is a worked example. Suppose, hypothetically, you tell an investor over coffee that a 60-unit building "should cost around 18 million." That number came from multiplying a rough unit cost by a unit count. Six months later the design has grown a level of underground parking and the cost consultant's Class 3 estimate is 23.5 million. The investor's memory is anchored at 18. To them, you have overrun by more than 30 percent before a shovel moved. To you, the project has not changed at all. Only the information has.

Second worked example. If the 18 million figure had been stated as "a Class 5 concept figure, range roughly 14 to 30 million, based on 60 units at a typical unit cost, excluding parking, dated March," the 23.5 million result would read as the estimate narrowing inside its range, not as an overrun. Same building, same cost, very different relationship with the investor.

What would have changed the outcome

Run the counterfactual, because that is where the transferable lesson sits. Four controls, each cheap compared with the overrun, would have changed the shape of this project. First, a frozen brief: a signed statement of the floor area and functions required, so that growth in either triggered a formal budget reset rather than a quiet revision. Second, a cost plan tied to that brief, prepared by an independent cost consultant and reissued at each design stage with its class stated. Third, stage gates, meaning formal decision points at which the owner either approves the next phase against an updated estimate or stops. Fourth, a deliberate choice of delivery method made with eyes open: if the owner chooses a route that keeps cost risk, the owner must also staff the controls to manage it. None of these require genius. All of them require someone with authority to say "we do not proceed until the number is reset." In a private project, that person is you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that an informal number escapes. It gets repeated, written into a board paper, quoted in a loan request, and becomes the baseline. The control is the rule below, applied without exception, including in conversation.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner gives a single number when asked "what will it cost?" because a range feels evasive. A range with a stated basis is the honest answer at an early stage, and it protects your credibility later.

Rule 13

No estimate leaves my hands, in writing or out loud, without its class, its date, its scope basis and its contingency stated alongside it.

Callback

In Week 3 you studied anchoring: the first number heard pulls every later judgement toward it. Holyrood is anchoring at national scale. The public anchored on the early range, and every later figure was experienced as a loss against it. The defence is to anchor people on the range and the basis, not on a point.

Recap

An early range was treated as a budget, the brief grew, the procurement route left the risk with the owner, and repeated revisions were not treated as a pattern. The rule: no estimate travels without its class, date, scope and contingency.

Next: Priya on how finance costs move total cost, yield on cost and value.
checklist: State the estimate class every time you quote a cost, including in conversation
Give a range with a basis at concept stage, never a single number
Write the scope basis and exclusions beside every figure
Date every estimate and name the drawing set behind it
Treat repeated upward revisions as a pattern, not as events
Reset the budget baseline formally when the brief grows
Know which party carries cost risk under the delivery method you chose
head: Field checklist
speak: Holyrood, the Scottish Parliament building, opened in 2004 at a reported cost of around four hundred and fourteen million pounds, roughly ten times the early range first put to the public. The early figure was a concept number for a smaller, simpler building, but it was treated as a budget. The owner chose a site and architect before the brief was settled, used construction management, which keeps cost risk with the owner, and started building while the design was still growing. Costs were revised upward again and again, and each revision was treated as a one-off rather than a pattern. The root cause was an early figure allowed to stand as a budget, with no stated class, scope or contingency. My rule is Rule 13: no estimate leaves my hands, in writing or out loud, without its class, its date, its scope basis and its contingency stated alongside it.
terms: Brief — the owner's written statement of what a building must contain and achieve, which the design is measured against.
Construction management — a delivery method in which the owner contracts with many trade packages directly while a manager coordinates them, leaving cost risk largely with the owner.
Baseline — the approved version of the budget or schedule that later performance is measured against.

hostile.q: You told us 18 million six months ago and now it is 23.5. Why should we trust the new number?
hostile.a: Because the new number is a different kind of number. The 18 was a concept figure from unit rates, without parking, and I should have given you the range and basis with it at the time; that is on me. The 23.5 is a Class 3 estimate from an independent cost consultant against the current drawings, with the scope, exclusions and contingency on page one. I will show you the reconciliation line by line, so you can see that the change is scope and information, not drift.

rule: Rule 13: No estimate leaves my hands, in writing or out loud, without its class, its date, its scope basis and its contingency stated alongside it.

title: Finance costs: the line that grows while you wait
summary: Finance costs are the one budget line that grows simply because time passes. This lesson shows how construction interest is estimated, why it is circular, and how a delay moves total cost, yield on cost and value.
body:
Finance costs are the only part of the budget that grows without anyone building anything. Every month of delay adds interest, and that interest is usually borrowed too.

Recall

Q. Why does an owner keep an owner decision log or reporting pack instead of relying on monthly memory?

A. Because reporting turns scattered facts into a record that lenders, partners and auditors can rely on. A good report shows budget, committed cost, cost to date and forecast side by side.

Q. What is net present value (NPV)?

A. The value today of a stream of future cash flows, discounted at a required rate of return, minus the investment. Positive NPV means the project beats the required return.

Q. What is the rule of three?

A. People remember points in threes. Give three reasons, three risks or three asks, and the listener can hold them.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a project runs late, the hard costs often hold, because the contract price is fixed. What does not hold is interest. Interest keeps accruing on every dollar drawn, the lender's fees may extend, and the building earns nothing. A developer who understands finance costs knows that a three-month delay is not a schedule problem. It is a cost problem with a known rate.

How construction interest is estimated

A construction loan is not drawn all at once. The lender advances money monthly as work is completed and certified. Early draws are small, the middle of the job draws heavily, and the last months are small again. Plotted as a running total, the drawn balance makes an S-shaped curve. So interest is charged on a balance that starts near zero and climbs to the full loan.

The practical shortcut is the average outstanding balance: the average amount drawn over the construction period, expressed as a share of the full loan. For a fairly even S-curve, practitioners often use something between 50 and 60 percent. That is a practitioner habit for early budgets, not a standard; once a draw schedule exists, compute interest month by month.

Worked example, all numbers hypothetical. Loan 15,275,000. Construction period 18 months. Interest rate 7 percent a year. Average outstanding balance 55 percent.

  1. Average drawn balance: 15,275,000 × 0.55 = 8,401,250.
  2. Annual interest on that balance: 8,401,250 × 0.07 = 588,088.
  3. For 18 months, multiply by 1.5 years: 588,088 × 1.5 = 882,131.

But the job does not end at construction completion. A rental building needs months to lease up, and during those months the loan is fully drawn and the building does not yet earn enough to cover interest. Add six months of lease-up at the full balance: 15,275,000 × 0.07 × 0.5 = 534,625. Add a lender's commitment fee of 1 percent, which is commercial practice and varies by lender: 152,750.

Total finance cost: 882,131 + 534,625 + 152,750 = 1,569,506. Round to 1,600,000 for the budget. That is the finance line carried in Day 1's sources and uses.

Say that out loud now.

The interest reserve and the circular calculation

An interest reserve is a portion of the loan set aside to pay the loan's own interest until the building produces income. Lenders usually require one, because they do not want interest payments to depend on the developer's personal cash flow during construction.

Here is the subtlety. If interest is paid from the loan, then the loan must be larger, which means more interest, which means a larger loan. It is a circular calculation. In a spreadsheet it shows up as a circular reference. Professionals solve it either by iterating until the numbers settle, which happens within a few rounds because each extra layer of interest is small, or by sizing the loan as a percentage of a total cost that already includes the interest. Never break the circle by simply deleting the interest. That is how budgets come up short.

How delay moves cost, yield and value

Second worked example. The project's stabilised net operating income (NOI), meaning the annual income after operating expenses once the building is leased and running normally, is a hypothetical 1,410,000. Total cost is 23,500,000. Yield on cost is 1,410,000 ÷ 23,500,000 = 6.0 percent. If similar buildings sell at a 5.0 percent capitalisation rate, value is 1,410,000 ÷ 0.05 = 28,200,000. The gap between value and cost, 4,700,000, is the development profit.

Now the building finishes six months late. Hard costs are fixed by contract. But the loan is now outstanding at the full balance for six more months: 15,275,000 × 0.07 × 0.5 = 534,625 of extra interest. Total cost rises to 24,034,625. Yield on cost falls to 1,410,000 ÷ 24,034,625 = 5.87 percent. Profit falls by the same 534,625 to about 4,165,000, a drop of more than 11 percent, from interest alone, with nothing physical going wrong. Add an extended general conditions bill from the contractor and the extension fee a lender may charge, and the damage grows.

The debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), meaning NOI divided by annual debt payments, does not change from the delay itself, because stabilised NOI is the same. What changes is your cushion: the extra interest usually comes out of contingency or out of new equity.

Rate risk on a floating loan

Many construction loans carry a floating rate, meaning a rate that moves with a published benchmark. Your interest estimate is then a guess about that benchmark. Test it. Using the same hypothetical numbers, a rise of one percentage point, from 7 to 8 percent, adds interest on the average drawn balance during construction, 8,401,250 × 0.01 × 1.5 = 126,019, and on the full balance during lease-up, 15,275,000 × 0.01 × 0.5 = 76,375. Together that is about 202,000 of extra cost for one point of rate. Write that sensitivity on the budget page: each one-point rise costs roughly 200,000. If that number frightens you, you have learned something about how much contingency or hedging the project needs. Hedging, meaning a contract such as an interest rate cap that limits how high the rate can go, is covered in Week 36. For now, the habit is to know the cost of one point before you sign.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. During construction, your equity in the project is carried at cost, not at the value you hope for. Until the building is stabilised, the 4,700,000 profit is a forecast, not an asset. More importantly, if the lender has required a personal guarantee covering cost overruns or interest shortfalls, a delay can become a call on your personal liquidity. Count that guarantee as a contingent liability, an obligation that only crystallises if something goes wrong, and hold a cash reserve that could meet a realistic delay. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an interest reserve sized for the scheduled finish date only. When the schedule slips, the reserve runs dry and the lender looks to you. The control is to size the reserve for a realistic delay, and to test the budget at three and six months late before you sign the loan.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner budgets interest on the full loan for the whole construction period, or on nothing at all. The first overstates cost and kills good deals. The second understates it and sinks them. Use the S-curve and the lease-up period.

Callback

In Week 11 you learned the time value of money. Finance cost is that principle billed monthly. A dollar of profit arriving six months later is worth less, and on top of that the delay charges interest to get there. Delay hurts twice.

Recap

Construction interest is charged on an S-shaped drawn balance; estimate it with an average outstanding balance, then add lease-up interest and fees. Funding interest from the loan creates a circular calculation that must be solved, not deleted. Every month of delay raises cost and cuts yield on cost and profit.

Next: LEX on the rules that govern a budget once someone else relies on it.
checklist: Estimate construction interest on an S-curve average balance, not the full loan
Add interest for the lease-up period at the full drawn balance
Include lender fees, and extension fees if the schedule may slip
Solve the interest circularity by iteration; never delete interest to break it
Size the interest reserve for a realistic delay, not the scheduled date
Test total cost and yield on cost at three and six months late
Record any personal guarantee as a contingent liability on your own balance sheet
head: Field checklist
speak: Finance cost is the only budget line that grows while nothing is being built. A construction loan is drawn in monthly steps that make an S-shaped curve, so interest is charged on a balance that climbs from near zero to the full loan. For an early budget, estimate the average outstanding balance at roughly half the loan, apply the rate for the construction period, then add interest on the full balance during lease-up, plus lender fees. Because interest is usually paid from the loan, the loan grows to cover its own interest, which is a circular calculation to solve, not delete. On a hypothetical 23.5 million project earning 1.41 million of stabilised income, a six-month delay adds about 535,000 of interest, pushes yield on cost from 6.0 to about 5.9 percent and cuts profit by more than 11 percent. So I size the interest reserve for a realistic delay, not the scheduled date.
terms: Average outstanding balance — the average amount of a construction loan drawn over the build, used to estimate interest before a draw schedule exists.
Interest reserve — part of a loan set aside to pay the loan's own interest until the property earns enough to cover it.
Contingent liability — an obligation, such as a guarantee, that only becomes payable if a specified event occurs.

hostile.q: Your interest reserve runs out the month after scheduled completion. What happens if you are three months late?
hostile.a: We have tested that case. Three months late adds about 270,000 of interest at the current rate. The budget covers it from construction contingency without reducing the field allowance below what our cost consultant recommends, and we have an equity commitment letter for an additional reserve if contingency is needed for field conditions instead. I would rather size the reserve to the delay case now than ask you for a modification later.

title: When someone relies on your budget
summary: A pro forma is your private working tool until you hand it to a lender or investor. From that moment it becomes a representation that others rely on. This lesson explains the legal concepts that govern that reliance and how to present a budget that is honest and defensible.
body:
The moment you hand a budget to a lender or investor, it stops being a private calculation and becomes a statement that someone else may rely on, with legal consequences if it is wrong.

Recall

Q. What does it mean to capitalise a cost?

A. To record it as part of the asset's value on the balance sheet rather than as an expense in the period. Development costs, including construction interest in many reporting frameworks, are typically capitalised into the property.

Q. How do the three financial statements connect?

A. Profit from the income statement flows into equity on the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement explains how the cash balance moved. Each one checks the others.

Q. What is the difference between hearing and listening?

A. Hearing receives the words. Listening tests what they mean and what is behind them, often by restating them back before replying.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, no statute says "a pro forma must be accurate." But a pro forma handed to someone who uses it to lend or invest can create exposure under general principles of contract, misrepresentation, and, if investors are involved, securities law. Nothing in this lesson is a jurisdictional conclusion. It teaches the concepts so you can recognise when to call a lawyer. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed where the project is located, and where investors are involved, securities counsel.

Representations and reliance

A representation is a statement of fact made to persuade someone to enter a deal. "The land is zoned for residential use" is a representation. "Our hard cost estimate, prepared by an independent quantity surveyor against the issued-for-tender drawings, is 15,000,000" is also a representation, of how the estimate was made. Reliance is the other party acting on that statement. When a lender sizes a loan from your budget, it is relying on it.

In general terms, legal systems derived from English common law, which you met in passing in earlier lessons and will study properly in Week 19, recognise that a false representation that induces a contract can give the other party remedies. The seriousness usually depends on your state of mind: whether the statement was made innocently, carelessly or knowingly. The specific tests and remedies differ by jurisdiction. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Forecasts are different, but not free

A forecast is not a statement of fact. "We expect stabilised net operating income of 1,410,000" is an opinion about the future. Courts in many systems treat genuine forecasts more leniently than false facts. But a forecast can still carry an implied statement of fact: that you believe it, and that you have reasonable grounds for it. A forecast you know to be stale, or built on a number you know to be wrong, can be treated as a misrepresentation of your belief.

Worked example. Hypothetically, your cost consultant updates the hard cost estimate from 15,000,000 to 16,200,000 on a Monday. On Wednesday you send the lender the old budget at 15,000,000 because the new one "isn't final." The lender relies on it. You have not merely shared a forecast. You have shared a number you had grounds to believe was wrong. The fix is simple and costs nothing but discomfort: send the current number with a note that it is under review.

Say that out loud now.

What the lender's documents usually add

In commercial practice, which varies by lender, a construction loan commitment usually requires the borrower to deliver a budget, often reviewed by a lender's independent cost consultant, and to warrant that the information provided is true and complete. Loan agreements commonly contain an in-balance requirement: the undisbursed loan plus the borrower's remaining equity must be enough to finish the project. If the budget proves short, that clause can stop draws until you put in more money. Some lenders treat a material inaccuracy in information provided as an event of default. These are contract terms, not law, and their exact wording is negotiated. Read them with your lawyer.

When investors are involved, a budget in an offering document can carry heavier consequences. Many jurisdictions impose liability for misrepresentation in materials used to sell an investment, sometimes with limited defences. Securities concepts are covered in Weeks 70 and 71. For now, the rule is: never put a pro forma in front of a prospective investor without securities counsel reviewing how and to whom it is being offered.

Who stands behind which number

A professional budget is a stack of other people's opinions, and you should know who stands behind each layer. The hard cost estimate is the cost consultant's professional opinion. The finance assumptions are yours, informed by the lender's term sheet. The land cost is a contract price. The soft costs are a mixture of signed fee proposals and your own allowances. In commercial practice, lenders often ask the cost consultant for a reliance letter, a document in which the consultant agrees that the lender may rely on its report. That shifts some responsibility for the hard cost opinion onto a party with professional standards and insurance. It does not remove yours for the rest of the budget. A useful habit is to mark each line in your working file with its source: contract, quote, consultant opinion or owner allowance. When a line is challenged, you can say at once whose number it is and how firm it is. Owner allowances deserve the most scrutiny, because they are the lines nobody else has checked.

How to present a budget that is defensible

Second worked example. Compare two cover notes for the same budget.

Version A: "Total project cost 23,500,000. All figures are estimates only and may change."

Version B: "Total project cost 23,500,000, dated 15 March. Hard costs from an independent quantity surveyor's Class 3 estimate against the 60 percent design development drawings. Hard cost contingency 5 percent, soft cost contingency 5 percent. Finance costs assume 7 percent interest on a 55 percent average drawn balance over 18 months plus six months of lease-up. Exclusions: tenant fit-out, off-site municipal works, cost escalation beyond the 12-month tender window. Known open items: geotechnical report pending."

Version A relies on a disclaimer. Disclaimers help, but in many systems a general disclaimer may not protect you from a statement you knew or should have known was wrong. Version B does something better: it tells the reader exactly what the number is and what it is not. A reader who relies on Version B relies on the right things. That is what makes a budget defensible: not legal language, but disclosed basis, assumptions, exclusions and open items.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a gap between what you know and what you have sent. The control is a version log: every budget sent outside the company carries a date and version number, and you record who received it. When the number changes materially, the people who received the old one receive the new one, promptly and in writing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes the phrase "estimates only" makes a budget safe to send in any state. It does not. Accuracy and disclosure protect you; boilerplate does not replace them.

Callback

In Week 6 you learned the line "I'll confirm by Friday." That line is legal hygiene as much as communication. When you do not know whether a number is current, the defensible answer is not to guess and not to send the old file. It is to commit to a dated confirmation and then deliver it.

Recap

A budget shared with a lender or investor is a representation others rely on. Forecasts carry an implied statement that you believe them on reasonable grounds. Loan documents add warranties and in-balance tests. Disclose the basis, assumptions, exclusions and open items; update recipients promptly when the number changes; and use a lawyer before anything goes to investors.

Next: Quincy builds a sources and uses table from a gross floor area, step by step.
checklist: Every budget sent outside the company carries a date and version number
The cover note states the estimate class, drawing set and contingency
Assumptions behind finance costs are written out
Exclusions and known open items are listed
A record shows who received each version
Recipients get the new number promptly in writing when it changes materially
A lawyer reviews loan warranties and in-balance clauses before signing
Securities counsel reviews anything shown to prospective investors
head: Field checklist
speak: A budget is your private tool until you hand it to a lender or investor. From then on, it is a representation that someone relies on. A false statement of fact that induces a deal can give the other side remedies, and how serious that is usually depends on whether you were innocent, careless or knowing. Forecasts are treated more gently, but they still imply that you believe them and have reasonable grounds. Sending an old number when you already know the new one is not a forecast; it is a problem. Loan documents usually add warranties that information is true and an in-balance test that can stop draws if the budget proves short. My practice is a dated, versioned budget with its basis, assumptions, exclusions and open items on the cover, a record of who received it, and a prompt written update when it changes. Investors see nothing without securities counsel.
terms: Representation — a statement of fact made to persuade someone to enter a transaction.
Reliance — the other party acting on a statement, such as a lender sizing a loan from your budget.
In-balance requirement — a loan term requiring that remaining loan funds plus remaining equity are enough to finish the project.

hostile.q: Your budget says 'estimates only.' If it turns out to be short, why shouldn't we treat that as a misrepresentation?
hostile.a: Because we have not relied on the disclaimer; we have relied on disclosure. The cover note states the estimate class, the drawing set, the consultant, the contingency, the finance assumptions, the exclusions and the open items, dated and versioned. If any of those change materially you will hear from me in writing. And the in-balance clause in your commitment protects you either way: if the budget proves short, the equity comes first.

title: Building the budget from square metres
summary: This lesson builds a complete sources and uses table from a gross floor area and a unit count, step by step with units, then shows what happens to the equity when hard costs escalate after the loan is committed.
body:
A defensible budget is built from quantities, not from a total you wanted to hit. Start with the floor area and unit count, price them, add the other buckets, and only then see what the sources must be.

Recall

Q. What is the first bucket in a sources and uses table, and what goes in it?

A. Land: the purchase price plus acquisition costs such as legal fees, survey, title work and any land transfer tax that applies.

Q. What is a discount rate in a net present value calculation?

A. The rate used to convert future cash into today's dollars, usually the return you require given the risk.

Q. Why does presenting numbers aloud need pace and pause?

A. Because a listener cannot reread a spoken number. A pause after each figure lets it land before the next one arrives.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will be handed budgets by architects, contractors and consultants. The fastest way to test one is to rebuild its spine yourself in ten minutes: area, rate, buckets, contingency, finance, sources. If your rough rebuild lands near their figure, you have a basis for questions. If it lands far away, you know where to dig.

Three units appear throughout. Gross floor area (GFA) is the total built floor area measured to the outside of the walls, including corridors and stairs. Cost per square metre is cost divided by GFA. Cost per unit is cost divided by the number of apartments. All numbers below are hypothetical.

Step 1: Quantities

The building has 60 apartments. Average net area per apartment is 75 square metres. Add corridors, stairs, lobby, mechanical rooms and walls. A building-efficiency ratio of 75 percent, meaning 75 percent of the gross area is sellable or rentable, is a reasonable hypothetical for a mid-rise apartment block.

  • Net area: 60 units × 75 m² = 4,500 m².
  • Gross floor area: 4,500 m² ÷ 0.75 = 6,000 m².

Step 2: Hard costs

The cost consultant's rate, from a Class 3 estimate against design development drawings, is 2,500 per square metre of GFA, including site work and the contractor's overhead and profit.

  • Hard costs: 6,000 m² × 2,500 per m² = 15,000,000.
  • Hard cost contingency at 5 percent: 15,000,000 × 0.05 = 750,000.

Step 3: Soft costs and land

Soft costs on a project like this often run at a percentage of hard costs. Use 20 percent as a hypothetical, then replace it with line items as quotes arrive: design fees, permits, insurance, legal, marketing, developer fee.

  • Soft costs: 15,000,000 × 0.20 = 3,000,000.
  • Soft cost contingency at 5 percent: 3,000,000 × 0.05 = 150,000.
  • Land, including acquisition costs: 3,000,000.

Step 4: Finance costs

Using the method from Day 3: construction interest on a 55 percent average balance for 18 months, plus six months of lease-up interest at the full balance, plus a 1 percent fee, totals about 1,570,000. Carry 1,600,000.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Total uses and the checks

Add them up: 3,000,000 + 15,000,000 + 750,000 + 3,000,000 + 150,000 + 1,600,000 = 23,500,000.

Now the sanity checks, which are where a quantity surveyor earns the fee.

  • Total cost per unit: 23,500,000 ÷ 60 = 391,667.
  • Total cost per square metre of GFA: 23,500,000 ÷ 6,000 = 3,917.
  • Land per unit: 3,000,000 ÷ 60 = 50,000.
  • Soft costs as a share of total: 3,150,000 ÷ 23,500,000 = 13.4 percent.

Compare each against your own record of past projects, or against a cost consultant's benchmark data for your market. A per-unit figure far below comparable buildings is a warning, not good news.

Notice what each check tells you. Cost per square metre tests the construction rate and the design's efficiency together. Cost per unit tests the unit mix: a building of small apartments costs more per square metre but less per unit than one of large apartments. Land per unit tests whether the site price makes sense for the product. Soft costs as a share of total tests whether a whole category has been forgotten. If one check looks odd and the others look normal, the problem is usually in that single line. If several look odd together, suspect the area figure, because it feeds almost everything.

Step 6: Sources

The lender offers 65 percent loan-to-cost, which is commercial practice that varies by lender and market.

  • Loan: 23,500,000 × 0.65 = 15,275,000.
  • Equity: 23,500,000 − 15,275,000 = 8,225,000.
  • Check: 15,275,000 + 8,225,000 = 23,500,000. Sources equal uses.

Most construction lenders require equity to go in first, before the first loan draw. So the 8,225,000 is not spread across the job; it is spent at the start, on land and early costs.

Step 7: When the equity is spent

Because equity goes in first, it is useful to map where it lands. In this hypothetical, the 8,225,000 pays for the land, 3,000,000, then the soft costs needed to reach a building permit and loan closing, say 1,500,000 of design, permit and legal fees, which leaves 8,225,000 − 3,000,000 − 1,500,000 = 3,725,000 to fund the first hard costs before the lender advances a dollar. At 15,000,000 of hard costs over 18 months, that equity carries roughly the first three to four months of construction. Two practical consequences follow. First, your equity is at maximum risk early, before the building is out of the ground, which is exactly when ground conditions are unknown. Second, if equity arrives late from a partner, the job stops, because the lender will not fund until the equity is fully spent. Write the equity timing on a single line under the sources table, with the expected date of the first loan draw.

Second worked example: escalation after commitment

Escalation is the rise in construction prices over time. Suppose the tender is delayed and hard costs come in 4 percent higher. Soft costs, being budgeted as 20 percent of hard, rise with them in this simplified model. Finance costs are held, to isolate the effect.

  • Hard costs: 15,000,000 × 1.04 = 15,600,000.
  • Hard contingency at 5 percent: 780,000.
  • Soft costs at 20 percent of hard: 3,120,000.
  • Soft contingency at 5 percent: 156,000.
  • New total: 3,000,000 + 15,600,000 + 780,000 + 3,120,000 + 156,000 + 1,600,000 = 24,256,000.
  • Increase: 24,256,000 − 23,500,000 = 756,000.

Here is the lesson. The loan was committed at 15,275,000. The lender does not usually re-size it upward because costs rose; it applies the in-balance test from Day 4. So the whole increase falls on equity: 8,225,000 + 756,000 = 8,981,000. A 4 percent rise in hard costs became a 9.2 percent rise in your equity requirement, because the debt did not move. That is equity leverage working against you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a budget built backward from the answer someone wanted: a target total, then rates chosen to fit. The control is to always build forward from quantities and independent rates, and to show your sanity checks per unit and per square metre beside the total.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner uses net area instead of gross area when applying a cost rate, which understates hard costs by the efficiency gap. On this building that mistake would have priced 4,500 m² instead of 6,000 m², missing 3,750,000. Always confirm which area a rate applies to.

Callback

In Week 12 you met work in progress: costs incurred on an asset not yet finished. The budget you built today is the plan for that work-in-progress account. Each month, cost to date plus cost to complete should be compared to this budget, bucket by bucket. The budget is the yardstick; the accounts are the measurement.

Recap

Quantities first: units, net area, efficiency, gross area. Price hard costs on gross area, add contingency, soft costs, land and finance. Check per unit and per square metre. Size the loan, and remember that cost increases after commitment usually fall on equity, magnified.

Next: Priya in the room with a lender's credit officer reviewing this budget.
checklist: Confirm whether each cost rate applies to gross or net area
Derive gross floor area from net area and a stated efficiency ratio
Build hard costs forward from quantities and independent rates
Show cost per unit and per square metre beside the total
Check land and soft costs as a share of total cost
Confirm sources equal uses after sizing the loan
Model a 4 percent hard cost rise and its effect on equity
Know that equity usually goes in before the first loan draw
head: Field checklist
speak: I build a budget forward from quantities. Sixty units at 75 square metres net is 4,500 square metres. At 75 percent efficiency, gross floor area is 6,000. At a consultant's rate of 2,500 per square metre of gross area, hard costs are 15 million, plus 5 percent contingency. Soft costs at 20 percent of hard are 3 million, plus contingency. Land is 3 million and finance costs about 1.6 million. Total uses are 23.5 million: about 392,000 per unit and 3,900 per square metre, which I check against past projects. A 65 percent loan is 15.275 million, so equity is 8.225 million, and it goes in first. Then I test escalation: if hard costs rise 4 percent after the loan is committed, total cost rises 756,000 and, because the loan does not move, equity rises 9.2 percent. Rates on gross area, sanity checks beside the total, and stress the equity, not just the cost.
terms: Gross floor area (GFA) — the total built floor area measured to the outside of the walls, including circulation and service space.
Building efficiency — net rentable or sellable area divided by gross floor area.
Escalation — the increase in construction prices over time between an estimate and the actual purchase.

hostile.q: Your cost per unit is well below the last three comparable buildings in this market. Why?
hostile.a: I checked that before you did. Two reasons and one open item. First, our efficiency is higher because there is no underground parking; the comparables carry one level. Second, the unit mix is smaller, so cost per unit falls even though cost per square metre is within the comparable range. The open item is the geotechnical report; if it changes the foundation design, I will re-issue the budget with the new figure and the date.

title: The credit officer reviews your budget
summary: A scene in a lender's office: the credit officer works through your sources and uses. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question, and when to stay silent.
body:
In a budget review the lender is not testing your arithmetic. It is testing whether you know where the money could run short, and whether you will tell them before they find out.

Recall

Q. What is a hostile question, and the three-step answer to one?

A. A question designed to expose weakness. Acknowledge it, bridge to what matters, then answer directly with evidence.

Q. In the Holyrood case, what was the root cause?

A. An early figure was allowed to stand as a budget, without its class, scope or contingency, while the owner carried cost risk through the procurement route.

Q. What is the difference between cash and profit in a project?

A. Profit is a forecast or accounting result; cash is what is available to pay bills. Lenders lend against the plan for cash, not the profit.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a credit committee approves the loan, but the credit officer writes the memo that goes to that committee. The impression you leave in a ninety-minute budget review becomes a paragraph in that memo: "sponsor is knowledgeable and forthcoming," or "sponsor was vague on contingency." That paragraph moves pricing, covenants and sometimes the decision itself.

The setting

This is a hypothetical scene. A credit officer, two years from retirement and very careful, has your sources and uses, the cost consultant's report and the draw schedule. The lender's independent cost consultant has already reviewed the budget and raised three comments. You have read those comments. That is your first preparation step: never walk into a budget review without having read the lender's consultant report line by line.

The questions, and the question behind each

"Walk me through your contingency." Behind it: is the contingency real money for real risk, or a plug to make the numbers work? Say: "There are two. Design contingency is now small because the estimate is against design development drawings. Construction contingency is 5 percent of hard costs, 750,000, for field conditions. The biggest single field risk is ground conditions, and the geotechnical report is due on the 30th." Never say: "That's just padding, we won't need it." If you say that, the officer hears that you will spend it on something else and then ask for more.

"Your interest reserve ends one month after scheduled completion." Behind it: when this runs late, who pays? Say: "We tested three months late. It adds about 270,000. That comes from contingency, and if contingency is consumed by field conditions instead, the equity commitment covers it. I can give you the delay case in writing today." Never say: "We won't be late." Every lender has heard it, and every one of them has seen a project that was.

"Your soft costs look light." Behind it: have you forgotten something you will need to fund later? Say: "Tell me which line you're comparing, and I'll show you the build-up." Then listen. The officer may be comparing to a project with a different scope. Or may be right.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example: answering with numbers aloud

The officer asks: "What does a 5 percent hard cost overrun do to you?" You have prepared. Speak it in three short sentences, pausing after each number. "Five percent of hard costs is 750,000. That consumes the whole construction contingency. Beyond that, the in-balance test means the next dollar is equity, and we have 500,000 committed above the budget for exactly that." Three sentences, three numbers, one conclusion. The officer can write that down verbatim, which is what you want.

Second worked example: the number you do not know. The officer asks the developer fee as a percentage of hard costs. You do not have it to hand. Say: "It's a fixed 600,000. I'd rather not guess the percentage aloud; I'll send it with the revised summary this afternoon." The percentage is 600,000 ÷ 15,000,000 = 4 percent, and you send it by email that afternoon as promised. A promised confirmation that arrives on time builds more trust than a quick answer that later proves wrong.

Third worked example: the comment you disagree with. The lender's consultant has written that hard costs look 3 percent light against its database. Do not argue the database. Say: "I've read the comment. Our consultant's rate is 2,500 per square metre on gross area. If your consultant is comparing to a building with underground parking, the gap closes. If not, I'd like the two consultants to reconcile line by line before the committee date, and I'll accept the higher figure if ours can't be supported." That answer concedes nothing you cannot defend, offers a process, and signals that your interest is in an accurate number rather than a cheap one.

After the meeting

The meeting is not over when you leave the room. Within the same day, send a short written note: what was asked, what you committed to send and by when, and any figure you corrected during the meeting. Keep it factual and unadorned. The credit officer will often lift sentences from it straight into the credit memo, which is the best outcome you can engineer. Then deliver every item on the date you named. A sponsor who sends four promised items on time has demonstrated the exact behaviour a lender wants during construction, when monthly reporting and draw requests will depend on the same reliability.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you state a number. Junior sponsors fill the pause with justification, and the justification usually introduces a new doubt. State it, then wait. Stay silent too while the officer reads. Do not narrate the page they are reading. And stay silent when the officer is working out a calculation aloud; let them finish, then confirm or correct.

The lines never to say

  • "The contractor guaranteed the price." A fixed-price contract is not a guarantee against claims, changes and insolvency.
  • "Everyone uses 5 percent." The officer is not asking what everyone does. They are asking what this project needs.
  • "We can always value-engineer it later." This tells the lender the design is not yet the design.
  • Any number you have not checked.

Holding your state

A careful credit officer may sound sceptical by habit, not because of you. If you feel the pressure rise, slow your speech, lower your pitch slightly and take one normal breath before answering. If you are on a night-shift rotation, schedule the review for the start of a rest period, not the end of a run of nights. You learned in Week 4 that judgement degrades with sleep debt. A budget review is not the meeting to prove you can run on empty.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is defending a number you privately doubt. The officer will usually sense it, and the memo will record it as evasion. The control is preparation: before the meeting, list the three weakest lines in your own budget and decide what you will say about each. Raise the worst one yourself before you are asked.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the review as a negotiation to win. It is an examination to pass. You negotiate terms in a different meeting, once the credit memo reads well. Arguing every comment in the review makes the officer write "sponsor was defensive," which costs more than any single comment could.

Callback

In Week 3 you learned that trust is built through credibility, reliability and visible openness about self-interest. Raising your own weakest line first is that principle in practice. It costs you a moment of discomfort and buys you the officer's belief in everything else you say.

Recap

Read the lender's consultant report first. Answer the question behind the question. Speak numbers in short sentences and stop. Never guess; confirm by a stated time and deliver. Raise your weakest line yourself.

Next: Kema's review of the week, with a Red Pen drill on a flawed sources and uses.
checklist: Read the lender's cost consultant report line by line before the meeting
List the three weakest lines in your own budget and prepare an answer for each
Raise the worst line yourself before you are asked
Prepare the delay case and the overrun case in writing
State numbers in short sentences, then stop talking
Never guess a figure; confirm by a stated time and deliver
Schedule the review at the start of a rest period, not the end of a run of shifts
head: Field checklist
speak: In a budget review, the credit officer is testing two things: whether I know where the money could run short, and whether I'll say so before they find it. So I read the lender's own cost consultant report first, and I list the three weakest lines in my budget and raise the worst one myself. When asked about contingency, I explain what it is for and name the biggest field risk; I never call it padding. When asked about delay, I give the tested number and who pays it. I speak numbers in short sentences, pause after each, and then stop talking. If I don't know a figure, I don't guess. I say when I'll send it, and I send it then. The officer's memo will say I was knowledgeable and forthcoming, and that paragraph moves pricing and covenants more than any argument I could make.
terms: Credit officer — the lender's employee who analyses a loan request and writes the recommendation for the credit committee.
Credit memo — the written analysis and recommendation that a lender's approving committee reads before deciding a loan.
Value engineering — changing a design or specification to reduce cost while keeping the required function.

hostile.q: If I gave you this loan and the job ran 10 percent over, where exactly would the money come from?
hostile.a: Ten percent of hard costs is 1,500,000. The first 750,000 comes from construction contingency. The next 500,000 is covered by the equity commitment above the budget, which is in the term sheet. That leaves 250,000, which would come from deferring the developer fee, and I am prepared to subordinate the fee in writing so that it is clear it comes behind your loan.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 13 review: cost, contingency and class
summary: Six questions and answers on the cost side of the pro forma, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a flawed sources and uses, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one idea: a budget is only as good as the information behind it, and that information must be visible on the page.

Recall

Q. What does yield on cost measure?

A. Stabilised net operating income divided by total project cost. It tells you the return the completed building earns on what it cost to build.

Q. What is the difference between a fixed cost and a cost that grows with time in a project?

A. A fixed-price contract holds hard costs steady, but interest and some soft costs, such as insurance and management, accrue every month the project runs.

Q. What is the point of a one-page memo?

A. To force a clear conclusion and its support onto one page, so a busy decision-maker can act on it without a meeting.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, review is where learning is fixed into memory. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer. Retrieval, the act of pulling an answer from memory, strengthens recall far more than rereading.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four buckets of uses. Answer: land, hard costs, soft costs and finance costs. Every cost belongs in exactly one.

Question 2. What is the test that sources and uses must pass? Answer: total sources equal total uses, to the dollar. If they do not, the difference is a funding gap.

Question 3. What does an estimate class tell you? Answer: how mature the design and information behind an estimate are, and therefore how wide its likely error range is. A concept-stage estimate needs much more contingency than one based on a nearly complete, priced design.

Question 4. State Rule 13. Answer: no estimate leaves my hands, in writing or out loud, without its class, its date, its scope basis and its contingency stated alongside it.

Question 5. Why is construction interest a circular calculation? Answer: interest is usually funded from the loan, so the loan must grow to pay it, which creates more interest. Solve it by iterating, never by deleting the interest.

Question 6. If hard costs rise 756,000 after a 15,275,000 loan is committed, who pays? Answer: usually the equity, because the in-balance test requires remaining loan plus remaining equity to finish the job. On an 8,225,000 equity base, that is a 9.2 percent increase.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Day 1 built the sources and uses and introduced contingency and estimate classes. Day 2 showed, through Holyrood, how an early figure drifts into a budget and why every estimate must travel with its class, date, scope and contingency. Day 3 priced finance costs on the S-curve and showed that delay raises cost while nothing is built. Day 4 explained that a shared budget is a representation others rely on, and that disclosure, not boilerplate, makes it defensible. Day 5 built the budget forward from square metres and showed escalation landing on equity. Day 6 put you in the room with a credit officer.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical budget summary and find the defects before reading on.

Project budget, 48 units. Total uses 17,900,000: land 2,500,000; hard costs 12,000,000 (5,000 m² net at 2,400 per m²); contingency 10 percent on land and hard costs, 1,450,000; soft costs 1,950,000. Sources: construction loan 11,700,000 (65 percent), equity 6,000,000. Interest to be paid from operating income. Budget firm; contractor has confirmed the price.

The defects:

  1. Sources do not equal uses. 11,700,000 + 6,000,000 = 17,700,000 against uses of 17,900,000. There is a 200,000 funding gap, unexplained.
  2. The hard cost rate is applied to net area. 5,000 m² is net. At a 75 percent efficiency, gross area would be about 6,667 m², and hard costs about 16,000,000, not 12,000,000.
  3. Contingency is applied to land. Land is a known, contracted price. Contingency belongs on what is uncertain: hard and soft costs.
  4. There are no finance costs. "Interest to be paid from operating income" is impossible during construction, when there is no operating income. Interest during construction and lease-up, plus fees, is missing entirely.
  5. No estimate class, date or drawing set is stated, and "budget firm" is an assertion with no basis. A confirmed price from a contractor is not proof against changes, claims or insolvency.

Count how many you found unaided. Four or five is the standard for this week.

Now correct it, because finding defects is only half the skill. Rebuild hard costs on gross area: 6,667 m² × 2,400 = about 16,000,000. Move contingency off land and onto hard and soft costs: 5 percent of 16,000,000 is 800,000, and 5 percent of 1,950,000 is about 98,000. Add finance costs; using the Day 3 method, a project of this size might carry something in the order of 1,300,000, which you would confirm against a draw schedule. The corrected total is roughly 2,500,000 + 16,000,000 + 800,000 + 1,950,000 + 98,000 + 1,300,000 = 22,648,000, against the 17,900,000 first stated. The original memo was not slightly optimistic. It was short by more than a quarter, and every defect pointed the same way, which is the pattern to look for: errors in an honest budget fall on both sides, while errors that all flatter the answer usually signal a budget built backward from a target.

Boardroom drill

Your task: explain the cost side of a pro forma to a board of non-specialists in two minutes. Stand, set a timer, and speak. Then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "Our project costs 23.5 million, and here is where every dollar goes. Three million for the land. Fifteen million to build it, with 750,000 set aside for problems we will find in the ground and the field. Three million for design, permits, insurance and fees, with a small reserve. And 1.6 million for the cost of borrowing while we build and lease up. That money comes from two places: a 15.3 million construction loan and 8.2 million of our equity, which goes in first. The estimate is Class 3, from an independent cost consultant, against drawings that are about 60 percent complete, dated this month. Our biggest open risk is ground conditions; the geotechnical report is due on the 30th. If the job runs three months late, it costs about 270,000 of extra interest, which our contingency covers. If costs rise after the loan is signed, our equity covers it, so we hold a reserve above the budget."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after a week like this is knowing the vocabulary without the habit. The control is to apply Rule 13 to the next cost figure you speak, at work or anywhere else, and notice how it changes the listener's reaction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reviews by rereading. Rereading feels productive and teaches little. Close the page, say the four buckets and Rule 13 aloud, and only then check. A second mistake is to skip the boardroom drill because it feels awkward to speak to an empty room. The awkwardness is the point. The first time you explain a budget aloud should not be in front of a lender who is deciding whether to fund you.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. Apply it to your budget. Imagine the money ran out in month fourteen. The most likely reasons are this week's lessons: a missing finance line, a contingency sized to the wrong class, an early figure mistaken for a budget, or escalation landing on equity.

Recap

Four buckets, balanced sources, contingency sized to the estimate class, finance costs on the S-curve, disclosure that makes a budget defensible, and a budget built from quantities. Rule 13 governs how any estimate travels.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was the cost side of the pro forma. Uses fall into four buckets: land, hard costs, soft costs and finance costs, and total sources must equal total uses to the dollar. Contingency is money for costs we cannot yet name, sized to the estimate class, which tells you how much we actually know. Holyrood showed what happens when an early figure is treated as a budget, which gave me Rule 13: no estimate leaves my hands without its class, date, scope basis and contingency. Finance costs grow with time, so delay raises cost while nothing is built. A budget handed to a lender is a representation, made defensible by disclosure, not disclaimers. Build costs forward from gross floor area. And remember that once the loan is committed, cost increases usually fall on equity, magnified. In the room, read the lender's consultant report first and raise your weakest line yourself.
terms: Retrieval practice — recalling information from memory without looking, which strengthens learning more than rereading.
Funding gap — the shortfall when total sources are less than total uses.
Pre-mortem — imagining in advance that a project has failed and working out the most likely reasons.

hostile.q: Your summary says the budget is firm because the contractor confirmed the price. What does 'firm' mean to you?
hostile.a: It means the hard cost line is under a fixed-price contract for the defined scope, nothing more. Changes, unforeseen conditions and contractor default can still move cost, which is why construction contingency is carried and why the in-balance test puts equity first. I should not have used the word 'firm' without that qualification, and the revised summary states the contract basis, exclusions and contingency instead.
